title: Helen “Hart of the Morning Star” Sells
summary: Setalcott leader and public-history contributor whose work connects community memory, museum interpretation and care for ancestral waters.
content:
Helen Sells is a Setalcott leader and contributor to public history. The Three Village Historical Society’s October 2025 statement names her and Robert “Silver Wolf” Thompson as co-chairs of the Setalcott Native American Council.1

Helping museums tell the story

The Long Island Museum credits Sells with helping develop its land acknowledgment, which the Setalcott Nation reviewed and approved. Its 2026 exhibition Enduring Heart: Native American Long Island also lists her on its advisory committee. These are concrete examples of Native participation in how institutions interpret Long Island.23

Community memory and care for the bay

At the April 24, 2025 opening of the improved Conscience Bay–Little Bay wetland area, Sells recalled childhood visits to the shore with her mother. She spoke alongside Thompson and youth committee chair A’riel “Thundering Sparrow” Hart. Their participation connects family memory with the Nation’s present-day environmental work.4

Read the community’s history together

Explore Setauket Ancestral Land and the related biography of Theodore Green. The map highlights public places connected with this work; it does not identify Sells’s home.

References
  1. Three Village Historical Society and Museum, Land Acknowledgment Statement, October 2025. Unpaginated; paragraphs naming Setalcott leaders and describing recorded elder interviews.
  2. The Long Island Museum, Land Acknowledgement Statement, undated, accessed September 17, 2026. Unpaginated; Setalcott approval and acknowledgment of Helen Sells’s contribution.
  3. The Long Island Museum, Enduring Heart: Native American Long Island, August 20–December 20, 2026. Unpaginated exhibition page; advisory committee listing Helen Sells.
  4. William Stieglitz, “Conscience Bay watershed site opens with Setalcott Nation as stewards,” TBR News Media, May 2, 2025; print edition May 1, 2025, p. A5. Report of April 24 opening and remarks by Helen Sells, Robert Thompson and A’riel Hart.
why_this_matters: Sells’s work shows that Indigenous history is shaped by living people: advising museums, sharing family memory and helping care for the waters of their homeland.
